Whose Tickets Are These?

One function computing three different where clauses, reused everywhere a ticket query needs to be scoped.

GET /tickets needs no authorize call (previous topic) — every role can reach it — but "every role sees the same list" is exactly wrong for a support desk: a customer should only ever see their own tickets; an agent should see their own assigned queue, plus whatever's still unclaimed; an admin should see everything. That's role-scoped queries, this lesson's other deliverable alongside protected routes, and it lives entirely in ticket.service.js, not in a controller or middleware:

// Figure 4.11: one where-clause fragment per role (src/services/ticket.service.js, excerpt)
const scopeForViewer = (viewer) => {
  if (viewer.role === 'customer') return { customerId: viewer.id };
  if (viewer.role === 'agent') {
    return { OR: [{ assignedAgentId: viewer.id }, { assignedAgentId: null }] };
  }
  return {};
};

Three branches, three different shapes of trust: a customer's fragment is the simplest possible ownership check — customerId must be theirs. An agent's is an OR — either it's already assigned to them, or assignedAgentId is null (nobody's claimed it yet, so it's fair game for any agent to see and potentially pick up). An admin's {} adds no restriction at all — an empty where fragment, which Prisma treats as "no filter," is precisely "sees everything."

viewer here is req.user (Lesson 4's authenticate), passed straight through from the controller — scopeForViewer never touches req itself, keeping this a plain function you could test with nothing but a { id, role } object (this lesson's testing topic does exactly that). The next slide is where this actually gets called.
